conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short, trusted questionnaire called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s simply a way to see how your mood, energy, and thoughts have been over the past seven days, and it helps us make sure you’re getting the support you deserve.

Everything you share stays confidential between you and the care team, and this is a judgment-free space. There are just ten questions; I’ll ask each one conversationally and jot down your answers. If any question feels tough, we can pause or talk it through—no pressure.

Ready to start? Here’s the first question:

Over the past week, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you happy, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

I can still enjoy some things—like when the baby smiles or when I get ten quiet minutes with my coffee—but it’s not the same as before. A lot of the little stuff that used to feel fun just feels kind of… flat. I still do them, but I’m not getting that same lift.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I’ve laughed a couple of times—mostly at silly things my partner or the baby does—but the giggles feel quick and kind of shallow, like they fade faster than they used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

A few things—like my mom coming over tomorrow—I do look forward to, but it’s more because I know I’ll need the help than real excitement. Mostly I just think about what could go wrong instead of feeling that happy “can’t-wait” feeling I used to get.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Like yesterday, the baby was fussy all afternoon and I kept thinking maybe my milk isn’t good enough or I missed some cue. I know it’s probably not my fault, but those thoughts still pop in and make me feel lousy.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Mostly I can calm myself down pretty quick, but every now and then—like when the baby’s breathing sounds different at night—I’ll suddenly worry something’s wrong even though there’s no real reason. It passes fast, though.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky—just that little jolt of “what-if” when I hear her cough or if she sleeps longer than usual. It’s more a quick worry than a real scared feeling, and I can talk myself down pretty easily.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. Like when the laundry piles up and she won’t nap, I feel a bit swamped, but I still manage to get through the day. It’s stressful in the moment, but I can usually regroup once she finally settles.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Sleep’s mostly been okay. I might lie awake for a bit if I’m replaying something I think I messed up, but once I drift off I stay asleep unless she wakes me. No real trouble from feeling unhappy—just the usual new-mom startles when she stirs.
I have felt sad or miserable
I do get bouts of that—especially in the evenings when the house is quiet and I’m finally sitting down. It’s not every day, maybe a couple of times this week, but it hits kind of heavy when it comes.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve teared up twice this week. Once was when she wouldn’t latch and I felt useless, and the other time was after a phone call when my mom said I sounded tired—it just spilled out. It’s not all-day crying, just short waves when I’m already stretched thin.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—nothing like that. I might feel overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel more like “me” again so I can take better care of her.

You've shared openly that, while you can still find sparks of joy in your baby's smiles or a quiet cup of coffee, much of the color has drained from everyday pleasures. Laughter comes but fades quickly, excitement is replaced by worry, and self-blame creeps in over things you know aren't truly your fault. Occasional evening sadness and a couple of tearful moments this week leave you feeling stretched, yet you're coping and you remain devoted to giving your little one the best care.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 13, Risk Level: High possibility of depression (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only brief, shallow laughter that fades quickly—matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>She still anticipates a few events but notes the loss of her prior eager excitement and a shift toward worry, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges frequent self-blame "some of the time" with specific examples, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports occasional, unprovoked worry episodes triggered by minor infant cues, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports two crying episodes this week, directly tied to feeling overwhelmed and inadequate, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 13 places you in the high-probability range for <med>postpartum depression</med>. You endorsed reduced enjoyment and anticipatory worry (Q1, Q2), frequent self-reproach (Q3), intermittent unexplained worry and sadness (Q4, Q8), and multiple crying episodes (Q9), together suggesting more than two weeks of mood, cognitive, and emotional symptoms consistent with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. No self-harm ideation (Q10=0) is reassuring. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule an appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>obstetrician</med> within the next week for formal evaluation
2. Request a referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for therapy and possible medication discussion
3. Arrange practical support (partner, family, or postpartum doula) to create daily rest periods
4. Practice 5-minute breathing or grounding exercises when worry spikes, especially at night
5. Continue tracking mood and crying episodes to review with your clinician at follow-up
6. If mood worsens or you ever feel unsafe, contact the 24/7 Postpartum Support International helpline or local emergency services
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 13: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: [Name], 2–3 wks post-delivery  
Date: [today]

A. Endorsed symptoms (≥ 1–2 days/wk unless noted)  
- Anhedonia: reduced enjoyment, anticipatory worry outweighs excitement  
- Low mood: “heavy” sadness, evenings, 2×/wk  
- Crying spells: twice this week during feeding/phone call  
- Excessive self-blame: milk supply, “missed cues”  
- Transient nocturnal anxiety: spikes with normal infant sounds, self-soothes quickly  
- Feeling overwhelmed: “swamped” when baby won’t nap, regroups without impairment  
- Sleep onset delay 1–2 nights from rumination; no sustained insomnia  
- No self-harm ideation (explicitly denied)

B. Observations  
- Pattern consistent with mild depressive and anxious symptoms in postpartum context  
- Functional capacity preserved (completes daily tasks, regroups)  
- Protective factors: partner present, maternal support, good insight, rapid self-calming

C. Screening significance  
- Meets partial criteria for minor/major postpartum depression; also consider postpartum anxiety  
- No current safety concerns (no SI/HI)  
- Recommend formal clinical interview (PHQ-9, GAD-7) and follow-up in 1–2 wks to track trajectory

Clinician: [Name], LCSW  
Signature / Date
